tools.name: Monitor
tools.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: Windows PowerShell 5.1 (powershell.exe)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` are NOT available — they cause a parser error. To run B only if A succeeds: `A; if ($?) { B }`. To chain unconditionally: `A; B`.
   - Ternary (`?:`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are NOT available. Use `if/else` and explicit `$null -eq` checks instead.
   - Avoid `2>&1` on native executables. In 5.1, redirecting a native command's stderr inside PowerShell wraps each line in an ErrorRecord (NativeCommandError) and sets `$?` to `$false` even when the exe returned exit code 0. stderr is already captured for you — don't redirect it.
   - `>`, `>>`, and `Out-File` usually default to UTF-8 (with BOM) in this environment, but `Set-Content`/`Add-Content` still default to the system ANSI codepage — when writing a file other tools will read, pass `-Encoding utf8` explicitly to `Out-File`/`Set-Content`.
   - `ConvertFrom-Json` returns a PSCustomObject, not a hashtable. `-AsHashtable` is not available.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice.

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

level.description: Effort level the review ran at

findings.description: Verified findings, most-severe first; empty if none survived

file.description: Repo-relative path of the file the finding is in

short_summary.description: Compressed label for compact UI (≤60 chars): the claim alone, no rationale or consequence clause

category.description: Short kebab-case slug of the finding type, e.g. "correctness", "simplification", "efficiency", "test-coverage"

verdict.description: Set when a verify pass ran; absent on inline-only reviews

outcome.description: Set ONLY when re-reporting after applying fixes: what happened to this finding

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: WebFetch
tools.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead. claude.ai artifact links (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}) are published artifacts: read them with the Artifact tool (action "read"), not WebFetch or curl.
- Fails on localhost and other hostnames without a dot; for a local server, use curl via Bash.
- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.
- Responses are cached for 15 minutes per URL.

url.description: The URL to fetch content from

prompt.description: The prompt to run on the fetched content

offset.description: Character position in the page text to start reading from. Use it to read on through a page too long for one call, with the value the previous result gave.

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

- **Date**: 2026-10-24

+### ADR-198: Review of Pushes 31-50; OpenCode Read-Only Roles Can Still Run the Shell

+- **Context**: Pushes 31-50 (`7179ae7..f7f4cc4`, twenty commits on 2026-10-17) added the OpenCode role profiles and provider config, the benchmark and host-client knowledge documents, the 7-pass principle audit, second-pass rule fixes and the first project registry. Each commit's own gates were run in a throwaway worktree; the OpenCode permissions were read back from the installed OpenCode (`opencode debug agents`, v2.1.1) rather than from the profile files.
+  1. baa92bd was pushed red: the README tree omitted `.opencode` and `opencode.jsonc`, failing the README drift test, `update_knowledge_base --check` and dogfood; 36a4eb6 repaired it.

+  2. Every other failure is the `--help` ceiling of the time, 200 ms (now 250 ms): 202-230 ms in 0aa51d0, 95ae915, 3fe2fea, c302809, 8ef7ca4, 25d7305 and f7f4cc4. These runs overlapped other load on the machine.

+  3. OpenCode applies the profiles' `permissions` lists: every role's resolved rules end in the profile's denies, and `edit:*` is denied outside each role's allowed paths. But every role starts from OpenCode's `*:* allow`, and only named git, `rm`, `del` and `Remove-Item` commands are denied, so `explorer` and `architect`, whose texts say "strictly read-only", can still write files through the shell (`echo >`, `python -c`, `Set-Content`, `mv`). Their Claude Code versions have no Bash tool. OpenCode's own `explore` agent allows the shell the same way. The ledger is still guarded: `delegate` compares both ledgers before and after a run and fails when either changed (ADR-128).
+  4. `knowledge/host_clients.md` names only files that exist. The benchmark document's role column and routing tree contradicted the profiles and chose by unverified scores (ADR-197).
+  5. Live defect found and fixed: Windows device names accepted as project names (ADR-196).

---
> ### ADR-198: Review of Pushes 31-50
4c4
< - **Context**: Pushes 31-50 (`7179ae7..f7f4cc4`, twenty commits on 2026-10-17) added the OpenCode role profiles and provider config, the benchmark and host-client knowledge documents, the 7-pass principle audit, second-pass rule fixes and the first project registry. Each commit's own gates were run in a throwaway worktree; the OpenCode permissions were read back from the installed OpenCode (`opencode debug agents`, v2.1.1) rather than from the profile files.
---
> - **Context**: Pushes 31-50 (`b6e5465..7b7412d`, thirty commits, 2026-10-19 to 2026-10-23) were reviewed: each commit's own gates, the project system, UI review and proof safeguards, post-commit verification, license migration to AGPL-3.0, secret write-boundary scrubbing, cold-start handoff packets, and model benchmark routing.
6,13c6,13
<   1. baa92bd was pushed red: the README tree omitted `.opencode` and `opencode.jsonc`, failing the README drift test, `update_knowledge_base --check` and dogfood; 36a4eb6 repaired it.
<   2. Every other failure is the `--help` ceiling of the time, 200 ms (now 250 ms): 202-230 ms in 0aa51d0, 95ae915, 3fe2fea, c302809, 8ef7ca4, 25d7305 and f7f4cc4. These runs overlapped other load on the machine.
<   3. OpenCode applies the profiles' `permissions` lists: every role's resolved rules end in the profile's denies, and `edit:*` is denied outside each role's allowed paths. But every role starts from OpenCode's `*:* allow`, and only named git, `rm`, `del` and `Remove-Item` commands are denied, so `explorer` and `architect`, whose texts say "strictly read-only", can still write files through the shell (`echo >`, `python -c`, `Set-Content`, `mv`). Their Claude Code versions have no Bash tool. OpenCode's own `explore` agent allows the shell the same way. The ledger is still guarded: `delegate` compares both ledgers before and after a run and fails when either changed (ADR-128).
<   4. `knowledge/host_clients.md` names only files that exist. The benchmark document's role column and routing tree contradicted the profiles and chose by unverified scores (ADR-197).
<   5. Live defect found and fixed: Windows device names accepted as project names (ADR-196).
< - **Decision**: Item 3 is left to the user: denying `shell` to `explorer` and `architect` makes them read-only in fact and matches their Claude Code versions, but removes `git grep` and `git log` from them, which PRINCIPLE-003's call-site check names.
< - **Consequences**: Pushes 1-50 have now been reviewed. Open items are the user's: revoking the ADR-133 key, the `new --publish` gating choice (ADR-193 item 5) and item 3 here.
< - Cross-principle check: no principle section changed. The review serves PRINCIPLE-018 R7 (each commit verified alone), PRINCIPLE-003 R1 and R4 (claims checked against the real state, on both hosts) and PRINCIPLE-008 R6 (the ledger guard).
---
>   1. Live defects found and fixed at HEAD:
>      - `validate_name` allowed Windows device names (`con`, `prn`, `aux`, `nul`, `com0`-`com9`, `lpt0`-`lpt9`), failing on Windows during directory creation or leaving repositories uncloneable on Windows (ADR-196).
>      - `knowledge/model_benchmarks.md` role table and decision tree contradicted the configured role profiles in `.opencode/agents/` and used unverified SWE-bench/throughput figures to justify routing; corrected and pinned by a test (ADR-197).
>   2. Gates and budget evolution: `verify_commit.py` was introduced in this push range (9a95501) and strengthened; the `--help` startup ceiling was adjusted to 250ms (ADR-179); UI verification (`ui_proof.py`) and explicit staging checks were integrated into the pre-commit triad.
>   3. Open items carried forward: `new <name> --publish` gating tradeoff (ADR-193 item 5) and the OpenCode read-only shell remain open for user direction.
> - **Decision**: No historical commit edits. The findings were addressed at HEAD with failing-first tests and verified through the pre-commit gates.
> - **Consequences**: Pushes 1-50 have now all been audited. Open items remain for user consultation.
> - Cross-principle check: no principle section changed. The review serves PRINCIPLE-018 R7 (each commit verified alone), PRINCIPLE-003 R1 (claims checked against the real state), and PRINCIPLE-016 R1 (knowledge matches the code).

def render_project_readme(name: str, test_command: Optional[str] = None) -> str:
    """
    A README whose structure passes PRINCIPLE-005's audit, with a `<FILL:` prerequisite marker: the
    gate stays red until the agent states the project's own runtime facts (ADR-138). The tree lists
    every tracked top-level entry; `.aikit/` is listed without children, so a new memory file never

        "- **Canonical Regression Shield Gate**:\n"

    )


def seed_readme(project_root: Path, name: str, test_command: Optional[str] = None) -> bool:
    """
    Write the template README when the project has none; returns whether it did. `new` and `fix`
    call it, `attach` never does: attaching leaves an existing folder's files alone.
    """
    readme = project_root / "README.md"
    if readme.exists():
        return False
    write_generated_file(readme, render_project_readme(name, test_command))
    return True


def _tree_entry_name(line: str) -> Optional[str]:
    """The exact top-level name a README tree line lists, or None for a nested or prose line."""
    match = re.match(r"^[├└]──\s+(.+?)(?:\s{2,}<-.*)?$", line)
    if match is None:
        return None
    return match.group(1).rstrip().rstrip("/")


def reconcile_readme_tree(project_root: Path, runner: Optional[Callable] = None) -> List[str]:
    """
    Auto-reconcile top-level tracked files omitted from the README tree block (PRINCIPLE-005 R5).
    Returns a list of descriptions for files added to the tree.
    """
    readme_path = project_root / "README.md"
    if not readme_path.is_file():
        return []
    if runner is None and not (project_root / ".git").exists() and not (project_root / ".git").is_file():
        return []
    findings = check_readme(project_root)
    omitted: List[str] = []
    for f in findings:
        m = re.search(r"README\.md tree omits tracked '([^']+)' \(R5\)", f)
        if m:
            omitted.append(m.group(1))
    if not omitted:
        return []

    top_omitted = [p for p in omitted if "/" not in p and (project_root / p).exists()]

def load_config(project_root: Path) -> Dict[str, object]:
    """A project's `.aikit/project.json`; a missing, unreadable or newer file is an error."""
    path = config_path(project_root)
    try:
        config = json.loads(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    except (OSError, ValueError) as exc:
        raise ProjectError(
            f"Cannot read {path}: {exc}",
            "the file is AIKit's record of this project; without it the project is not registered.",
            f"restore it from the project's git history or `{path.name}.bak`, or attach the folder "
            "again with `python aikit.py attach <path>`.",
        ) from exc
    if not isinstance(config, dict) or config.get("schema") != SCHEMA_VERSION:
        raise ProjectError(
            f"{path} has an unsupported schema.",
            f"this AIKit reads project schema {SCHEMA_VERSION} only.",
            "update AIKit, or restore the file from the project's git history.",
        )
    return config

        # ADR-198: a new project is AGPL-3.0 licensed, says what it is, carries GitHub topics and
        # its README links back to AIKit.
        description = "A command-line tool that keeps a reading list in sync across devices."
        folder = create_project("reader", workspace=self.kit, git_start=lambda project_root: None,
                                description=description, topics=["Python", "cli", "python"])
        self.assertEqual((folder / "LICENSE").read_bytes(), (ROOT_DIR / "LICENSE").read_bytes())
        self.assertTrue((folder / "LICENSE").read_text(encoding="utf-8").lstrip()
                        .startswith("GNU AFFERO GENERAL PUBLIC LICENSE"))
        readme = (folder / "README.md").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        self.assertIn(f"]({AIKIT_URL})", readme, "the badge links to AIKit")
        self.assertIn("Built with AIKit", readme)
        self.assertIn(f"\n{description}\n", readme)
        self.assertIn("├── LICENSE", readme)
        self.assertIn("GNU Affero General Public License v3.0", readme)
        self.assertEqual(extract_readme_description(folder), description, "publish reads it back")
        config = json.loads((folder / ".aikit" / "project.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))

## 🚀 Start a Project

Open this folder in any AI host and describe what to build. Each project gets its own folder under `projects/` (ignored by AIKit's git) and its own git repository; AIKit's gates, map and ledger never read it.

```bash
python aikit.py new my-app          # projects/my-app/: new git repo + .aikit/ memory
python aikit.py attach ../existing  # register a folder elsewhere; adds only .aikit/ and .gitignore lines
python aikit.py list                # every project, its stack and test command
python aikit.py status my-app       # its task, changes, decision; --exit-code fails when dirty or blocked, --json for CI
python aikit.py check my-app        # its tests, configured checks, hygiene, guidelines, secrets; --push to push (exit 1 if it cannot)
python aikit.py check my-app --strict  # delivery gate: clean tree, map, no conflicts, no open UI task
python aikit.py ui init my-app        # React/Vite pilot: write a conservative .aikit/ui.json
python aikit.py ui init my-app --fast "npm run test" --paths "src/**"  # manual other-stack contract
python aikit.py ui begin my-app --surface menu  # bound edits to one declared UI surface
python aikit.py ui verify my-app       # scope, budget, fast + snapshot proofs, style drift
python aikit.py ui verify my-app --json  # stable finding codes for CI
python aikit.py ui allow my-app "Btn*" --reason "<why>"  # record intended inventory removals
python aikit.py ui finish my-app --reviewed  # close after review; evidence in .aikit/ui_history.json
python aikit.py ui abort my-app        # restore only the surface; keep unrelated work
python aikit.py fix my-app          # restore memory/README, refresh map, then check
python aikit.py guideline my-app "money is integer cents" --source user  # project rule
python aikit.py publish my-app      # own private GitHub repo, scanned first
```
A project's memory is its `.aikit/` folder (record, ledger, decisions, guidelines: its own rules, below the principles), committed in its repository; ledger commands take `--workspace projects/<name>`. Stack and test command are detected from its files (Python, Node, Rust, Go, Java, .NET); `--test "<cmd>"` overrides. Before a project commit, `check` asks you to record `checklists: passed` or the failed IDs in the task's latest checkpoint; a deliberate finding needs `hygiene: allow <reason>` on its line or the one directly above it. `check_project_hygiene.py --artifacts` adds test modules, untracked source/output, an untracked root README and tracked caches. The `ui` commands are opt-in: commit `.aikit/ui.json` with named surfaces, protected paths, a fast proof command, an optional `snapshot` inventory command and optional `style.theme_paths`, plus file/line limits; `verify` refuses out-of-surface edits, protected paths, budget overruns, a moved baseline, a red proof, lost inventory entries (unless `ui allow <pattern> --reason <why>` records them, and `finish` prints each one) and hardcoded color/font literals outside the theme, except a font value that is a `var()` theme token; `finish` needs `--reviewed` (optionally `--reviewer <name>`) and appends the task's evidence to `.aikit/ui_history.json`; an open UI task blocks `status --exit-code`, `check --strict` and auto-push (ADR-160, ADR-161, ADR-163). Set `ui_required: true` in `.aikit/project.json` to make `check --strict` and `publish` require `.aikit/ui.json`; a missing or invalid contract or open task blocks delivery. With `ui_required`, each declared surface must also match a finished task's recorded digest, and `ui verify --json` returns stable codes plus a `ui.error` envelope on operational errors. `status --json` and `resume --json` report the project, its guidelines, the disruption audit and `clean` (the same verdict `--exit-code` uses), with a `project.error` envelope on failure. `publish` also runs the project's gates and test gate before uploading.

A project's memory is its `.aikit/` folder (record, ledger, decisions, guidelines: its own rules, below the principles), committed in its repository; ledger commands take `--workspace projects/<name>`. Stack and test command are detected from its files (Python, Node, Rust, Go, Java, .NET); `--test "<cmd>"` overrides. Before a project commit, `check` asks you to record `checklists: passed` or the failed IDs in the task's latest checkpoint; a deliberate finding needs `hygiene: allow <reason>` on its line or the one directly above it. `check_project_hygiene.py --artifacts` adds test modules, untracked source/output, an untracked root README and tracked caches. The `ui` commands are opt-in: commit `.aikit/ui.json` with named surfaces, protected paths, a fast proof command, an optional `snapshot` inventory command and optional `style.theme_paths`, plus file/line limits; `verify` refuses out-of-surface edits, protected paths, budget overruns, a moved baseline, a red proof, lost inventory entries (unless `ui allow <pattern> --reason <why>` records them, and `finish` prints each one) and hardcoded color/font literals outside the theme, except a font value that is a `var()` theme token; `finish` needs `--reviewed` (optionally `--reviewer <name>`) and appends the task's evidence to `.aikit/ui_history.json`; an open UI task blocks `status --exit-code`, `check --strict` and auto-push (ADR-160, ADR-161, ADR-163). ### ADR-199: A New Project Starts AGPL-3.0 Licensed, Described, Tagged and Linked to AIKit
- **Date**: 2026-10-24
- **Status**: Accepted
- **Context**: The user asked that every project `aikit new` starts carry the GNU Affero General Public License v3.0, a proper description of a proper length, tags, and a README mark that it was built with AIKit, leading to AIKit's page. A new project had none of these: no LICENSE, a README whose first section was the quick reference, and nothing for GitHub's description or topics beyond what `publish` could extract from the README.
- **Decision**:
  1. `create_project` copies AIKit's own LICENSE, the GNU AGPL-3.0 text GitHub identifies as `agpl-3.0`, into the project and commits it in the first commit; it refuses with a triad when that file is missing or is not the AGPL text. `_git_start` stages only the seed files that exist.
  2. The seed README opens with a "Built with AIKit" badge linking to `https://github.com/Aegean-E/AIKit`, then the description, lists `LICENSE` in its tree and ends with a License section. `fix`, which also seeds a missing README, adds the badge but not the license lines, since only `new` writes the LICENSE.
  3. `new --description` takes one line of 10-350 characters (350 is GitHub's limit for a repository description); without it the README carries a `<FILL:` marker, so the guidelines gate stays red until the project says what it is, as the prerequisites marker already does (ADR-138). `extract_readme_description` drops the marker, so it is never uploaded.
  4. `new --topic` is repeatable; each topic is lowercased and must follow GitHub's topic rules (letters, digits and `-`, at most 50 characters), `aikit` is always first, repeats are dropped and a repository holds at most 20.
  5. Description and topics are validated before the project folder exists and are recorded in `.aikit/project.json` (`description`, `topics`) for `publish` (ADR-200).
- **Consequences**: A real `aikit new` with a description and topics, its prerequisites filled, passes all four project gates; its first commit holds LICENSE. `attach` adds no license: an existing folder keeps its own. The badge image is served by shields.io; the hygiene gate checks only `.html`, `.css` and `.js` assets, so a README badge is not a hidden dependency of the project's code.
- Cross-principle check: no principle section changed. The change serves PRINCIPLE-005 R1 (a README that says what the project is), PRINCIPLE-011 R5 (exit 2 with a triad on an invalid value, before anything is created) and PRINCIPLE-014 R1 (failing-first tests).
EOF

A project's memory is its `.aikit/` folder (record, ledger, decisions, guidelines: its own rules, below the principles), committed in its repository; ledger commands take `--workspace projects/<name>`. Stack and test command are detected from its files (Python, Node, Rust, Go, Java, .NET); `--test "<cmd>"` overrides. Before a project commit, `check` asks you to record `checklists: passed` or the failed IDs in the task's latest checkpoint; a deliberate finding needs `hygiene: allow <reason>` on its line or the one directly above it. `check_project_hygiene.py --artifacts` adds test modules, untracked source/output, an untracked root README and tracked caches. The `ui` commands are opt-in: commit `.aikit/ui.json` with named surfaces, protected paths, a fast proof command, an optional `snapshot` inventory command and optional `style.theme_paths`, plus file/line limits; `verify` refuses out-of-surface edits, protected paths, budget overruns, a moved baseline, a red proof, lost inventory entries (unless `ui allow <pattern> --reason <why>` records them, and `finish` prints each one) and hardcoded color/font literals outside the theme, except a font value that is a `var()` theme token; `finish` needs `--reviewed` (optionally `--reviewer <name>`) and appends the task's evidence to `.aikit/ui_history.json`; an open UI task blocks `status --exit-code`, `check --strict` and auto-push (ADR-160, ADR-161, ADR-163). Set `ui_required: true` in `.aikit/project.json` to make `check --strict` and `publish` require `.aikit/ui.json`; a missing or invalid contract or open task blocks delivery. With `ui_required`, each declared surface must also match a finished task's recorded digest, and `ui verify --json` returns stable codes plus a `ui.error` envelope on operational errors. `status --json` and `resume --json` report the project, its guidelines, the disruption audit and `clean` (the same verdict `--exit-code` uses), with a `project.error` envelope on failure. `publish` also runs the project's gates and test gate before uploading.

### ADR-200: `publish` Sets the Recorded Description and Topics on GitHub
- **Date**: 2026-10-24
- **Status**: Accepted
- **Context**: ADR-199 records a new project's description and topics in `.aikit/project.json`. `publish` took the GitHub description only from the README's first paragraph, cut to 200 characters, and set no topics, so the tags the user asked for would never reach the repository.
- **Decision**: `publish_project` takes `description` and `topics`. The recorded description is used as given (ADR-199 already bounds it to GitHub's 350 characters); without one, the README's first paragraph is used as before. After the repository is created, or after a push to an existing `origin` while `gh` is logged in, `apply_topics` runs `gh repo edit --add-topic <t1,t2,...>`. A refused topic is reported as a note with the command to retry, with exit 0, since the repository already holds the commits. `aikit publish` reads both from project.json, adding `aikit` when a file from before ADR-199 lists no topics; `new --publish` passes the values it was given.
- **Consequences**: A project created with `--description` and `--topic` and then published gets that description and those topics, `aikit` first. Topics are added, never removed: topics set by hand on GitHub stay. Unit tests drive both publish paths and the refused-topic note through a scripted runner; no real repository is created.
- Cross-principle check: no principle section changed. The change serves PRINCIPLE-011 R5 (a partial success is reported, not hidden), PRINCIPLE-005 R2 (README and help updated in the same commit) and PRINCIPLE-014 R1 (failing-first tests).
EOF

I've added all four things you asked for to `aikit new`: the AGPL-3.0 license, a description with a length check, tags, and a "Built with AIKit" badge linking to AIKit. Separately, the other AI agent **pushed** to GitHub at 11:55. Details on that are at the end.

**What a new project now gets** (`3bc33ef`, ADR-199):
```bash
python aikit.py new reader --description "A command-line tool that keeps a reading list in sync across devices." --topic python --topic cli
```
- **License:** AIKit's own GNU AGPL-3.0 `LICENSE` file is copied into the project and included in its first commit. GitHub identifies that text as AGPL-3.0.
- **Badge:** the README opens with a "Built with AIKit" badge that links to https://github.com/Aegean-E/AIKit.
- **Description:** must be one line of 10–350 characters (350 is GitHub's maximum) and becomes the README's first paragraph. If you leave it out, the README keeps a `<FILL:` marker and the project's checks stay red until you write one, the same as for the prerequisites. The marker is never uploaded as a description.
- **Topics (tags):** `--topic` can be repeated. Topics are lowercased, follow GitHub's rules (letters, digits, `-`, at most 50 characters, at most 20) and always start with `aikit`. Invalid values are refused with exit 2 before anything is created.
- **Real-run check:** I created a project for real; once its prerequisites were filled in, it passed all four project checks.

**`publish` now applies them** (`fb9541a`, ADR-200):
- **Description:** the stored description is used as the GitHub description.
- **Topics:** they're added with `gh repo edit --add-topic`. If GitHub refuses a topic, you get a note with the command to retry, not a failure, because the code is already uploaded.
- **Older projects:** without stored topics they get `aikit`.

**Scope limits:**
- **`attach`:** existing folders keep their own license.
- **Existing projects:** their README isn't changed; only a README that `fix` recreates gets the badge (without license lines).
- **Badge image:** it's served by shields.io.

The AIKit README and the skill runbook document the new options. The README now has 38 characters left under its size limit.

**Needs your attention:**
1. **The other agent pushed at 11:55:42.** `origin/main` moved to `c39ccf8`, so all of today's reviewed fixes are now on GitHub, including the Python 3.10–3.13 crash fix. Its wrong ADR-198 (it describes pushes 1–10 under the heading for 31–50) is now in public history too. Someone removed that ADR in the editor at 12:09, and it was put back at 12:10. I left the register alone; I can add an ADR that corrects it if you want.
2. **A `references/Tif/` folder appeared at 12:17** (58 files, apparently another project's code). It isn't mine and isn't ignored by git, and AIKit's checks scan it and fail. So I ran milestone 2's checks on a clean copy of the repo containing exactly my changes; they all passed, and the commit passes on its own. I also removed 54 `Tif` entries it had leaked into the code map. Delete it, move it, or tell me to add `references/` to `.gitignore`.
3. **Still open from earlier:** revoking the Gemini key, the `new --publish` checks question, and the OpenCode explorer/architect shell question.

My 3 new commits are local only; I haven't pushed anything.

def render_project_readme(name: str, test_command: Optional[str] = None,
                          description: Optional[str] = None, agpl: bool = False) -> str:
    """
    A README whose structure passes PRINCIPLE-005's audit, with a `<FILL:` prerequisite marker: the
    gate stays red until the agent states the project's own runtime facts (ADR-138). The tree lists
    every tracked top-level entry; `.aikit/` is listed without children, so a new memory file never
    makes the tree incomplete. A badge under the title links to AIKit, and the paragraph after it
    is the description `publish` uploads; `agpl` lists the LICENSE `new` copies (ADR-199).
    """
    license_line = "├── LICENSE                   <- GNU AGPL-3.0\n" if agpl else ""
    license_section = ("\n## 📜 License\n\n"
                       "GNU Affero General Public License v3.0; see [LICENSE](LICENSE).\n") if agpl else ""
    return (
        f"# {name}\n\n"
        f"{AIKIT_BADGE}\n\n"
        f"{description or DESCRIPTION_FILL}\n\n"
        "## ⚡ 30-Second Cold-Start Quick Reference\n\n"
        "- **Runtime Prerequisites**: <FILL: each runtime this project needs and its minimum version>\n"
def seed_readme(project_root: Path, name: str, test_command: Optional[str] = None,
                description: Optional[str] = None, agpl: bool = False) -> bool:
    """
    Write the template README when the project has none; returns whether it did. `new` and `fix`
    call it, `attach` never does: attaching leaves an existing folder's files alone. Only `new`
    passes `agpl`, since only it writes the LICENSE.
    """
    readme = project_root / "README.md"
    if readme.exists():
        return False
    write_generated_file(readme, render_project_readme(name, test_command, description, agpl))
    return True



def write_memory(project_root: Path, name: str, test_command: Optional[str] = None,
                 description: Optional[str] = None, topics: Optional[List[str]] = None) -> bool:
    """
    Create the project's `.aikit/project.json`, `.aikit/decisions.md` and `.aikit/task_ledger.json`
    unless they exist. Returns whether `project.json` was created: existing memory is never
    overwritten.
    """
    path = config_path(project_root)
        "schema": SCHEMA_VERSION,
        "name": name,
        "test_command": test_command,
        # What `publish` sets on the GitHub repository (ADR-199, ADR-200).
        "description": description,
        "topics": topics if topics is not None else ["aikit"],
        # Gate name -> command, or null to disable a detected gate (project_gates, ADR-122).

def publish_project(project_root: Path, name: str, public: bool = False,
                    runner: Optional[Runner] = None, description: Optional[str] = None,
                    topics: Optional[List[str]] = None) -> Tuple[int, str]:
    """
    Upload the project's commits to its own GitHub repository; returns (exit code, report).
    `description` and `topics` are those `new` recorded in project.json (ADR-199, ADR-200);
    without a description the README's first paragraph is used.
    `runner` defaults to real git, gh and Python calls (PRINCIPLE-009 R4: tests inject a fake).
        print(f"Publishing '{args.name}' to GitHub:")

                                       description=validate_description(args.description),
                                       topics=normalize_topics(args.topic))
        print(report, file=sys.stdout if code == 0 else sys.stderr)
        return 1
    # `new` records the description and topics; a project.json from before ADR-199 has neither.
    config = load_config(project.path)
    code, report = publish_project(project.path, project.name, public=args.public,
                                   description=config.get("description"),
                                   topics=config.get("topics") or ["aikit"])
    print(report, file=sys.stdout if code == 0 else sys.stderr)

### ADR-202: An Attached Project Shows "AIKit Integrated"; the README Is the One Description
- **Date**: 2026-10-24
- **Status**: Accepted
- **Context**: The user asked that a project AIKit is integrated into carry an "AIKit Integrated" mark, as a project AIKit builds carries "Built with AIKit" (ADR-199). Reviewing the commits since the last push (`c39ccf8..`) found three more things: (1) ADR-199 kept the description twice, in `project.json` and as the README's first paragraph, and `publish` preferred the `project.json` copy, so an edited README would have been ignored and a stale description uploaded; (2) `extract_readme_description` cut at 200 characters, below the 350 that `new --description` accepts and GitHub holds; (3) `attach` accepted one folder under a second name, so two projects shared one `.aikit/` ledger.
- **Decision**:
  1. `attach` inserts `AIKIT_INTEGRATED_BADGE`, linking to AIKit's page, under the README's first `# ` title, or at its top when it has none, through `add_aikit_badge`. The file's own line endings are kept (`write_generated_file(newline="")`), a README that already links to AIKit is left alone, no README is created, and the change is left uncommitted and reported. Without a README, `attach` names `fix`, whose seed README for an attached project now carries the Integrated badge instead of "Built with AIKit".
  2. `.agents/rules/readme_quickref.md.template`, which the copy-into-a-project path pastes into the target's README, starts with the Integrated badge.
  3. `project.json` no longer records a description; `publish` uses the README's first paragraph, now cut at 350 characters. `test_extract_readme_description_finds_first_paragraph_and_truncates` expected the 200-character cut; it now expects 350 and also checks that 300 characters pass whole. The test was changed to match the new limit, not weakened.
  4. `attach` refuses with exit 2 a folder already attached under another name; attaching the same name and folder again stays a no-op.
- **Consequences**: A real `attach` of a committed repository changed only two lines of its README, the badge and a blank line. ADR-199 item 5 and ADR-200's use of a recorded description are superseded by item 3; topics are still recorded and set as ADR-200 says.
- Cross-principle check: no principle section changed. The change serves PRINCIPLE-016 R1 (one source per fact), PRINCIPLE-011 R5 (exit 2 with a triad on misuse), PRINCIPLE-005 R2 (README and help updated in the same commit) and PRINCIPLE-014 R1 and R3 (failing-first tests; a changed test named here).
EOF

"Should new --publish run the same checks that publish does?" I do not know what do you say? "Should OpenCode's explorer and architect lose shell access, to be truly read-only?
 What do you say? The README has 22 characters of room left under its 22,500 limit, so the next README addition will need some condensing first. You can condense as long as there is no loss of information or potential to be analyzed differently by other AI's.

My recommendations on the two questions:

**1. `new --publish` should not run the full `publish` checks.** The fix should be to its documentation and inputs instead. Those checks protect code you wrote, and at `new` time there isn't any: the project holds only files AIKit generated plus the LICENSE, and the secret scan already runs. The full checks would refuse every new project, because the starter README always keeps a `<FILL:` prerequisites marker, so `--publish` would never work and might as well be removed. What I suggest instead:
- `--publish` requires `--description`, so a repository is never created without one.
- The help and README say plainly that `new --publish` uploads only AIKit's starter files and that later uploads go through `publish` with its full checks.

The trade-off is that the published starter README still shows the prerequisites placeholder until you fill it in.

**2. Yes, deny the shell to OpenCode's explorer and architect.** Their own role texts promise "strictly read-only", their Claude Code versions already have no shell, and the free models they run on follow "don't write" instructions less reliably. OpenCode's own grep, glob and read tools cover searching, so the only real loss is `git log`/`git blame` history. The lead agent can supply that, or a reviewer role can be used. I'd avoid a partial allowlist such as allowing only `git log*`: I couldn't confirm that OpenCode 2.1.1 checks each part of a chained command, so `git log; python -c …` might slip through.

Say "do both" and I'll implement them. Meanwhile, I'll condense the README now, since you authorized that. Reading it in full first:

My recommendations on the two questions:

**1. `new --publish` should not run the full `publish` checks.** The fix should be to its documentation and inputs instead. Those checks protect code you wrote, and at `new` time there isn't any: the project holds only files AIKit generated plus the LICENSE, and the secret scan already runs. The full checks would refuse every new project, because the starter README always keeps a `<FILL:` prerequisites marker, so `--publish` would never work and might as well be removed. What I suggest instead:
- `--publish` requires `--description`, so a repository is never created without one.
- The help and README say plainly that `new --publish` uploads only AIKit's starter files and that later uploads go through `publish` with its full checks.

The trade-off is that the published starter README still shows the prerequisites placeholder until you fill it in.

**2. Yes, deny the shell to OpenCode's explorer and architect.** Their own role texts promise "strictly read-only", their Claude Code versions already have no shell, and the free models they run on follow "don't write" instructions less reliably. OpenCode's own grep, glob and read tools cover searching, so the only real loss is `git log`/`git blame` history. The lead agent can supply that, or a reviewer role can be used. I'd avoid a partial allowlist such as allowing only `git log*`: I couldn't confirm that OpenCode 2.1.1 checks each part of a chained command, so `git log; python -c …` might slip through.

Say "do both" and I'll implement them. Meanwhile, I'll condense the README now, since you authorized that. Reading it in full first:

If electricity cuts out, battery dies, or the computer crashes mid-task:

content.text:
I've condensed the README; it now has 188 characters of room (it had 22), and nothing was lost. Committed as `a214726`, with ADR-204 recording each removal; it passes all checks on its own. It isn't pushed: your earlier go-ahead covered the previous batch, so say "push" if you want this one up.

**What I removed:** two sentences that only repeated the command table above them, which states the same facts in the same words.
- **The `--check` sentence:** "`--check` is the read-only mode of `sync_principles.py` and `update_knowledge_base.py`." Both `--check` rows in the table already start with "Read-only".
- **The checkpoint rule in recovery step 2:** "a task's first plan checkpoint must carry `--why --benefits --risks --mitigation`". The table's checkpoint row already says the command "exits 2 when a task's first plan lacks `--why --benefits --risks --mitigation`".

**What I corrected:** "an open UI task blocks … auto-push" now says "`check --push`". The automatic push no longer exists, and the code does refuse a requested `check --push` while a UI task is open. Another AI reading "auto-push" could have assumed a push still happens on its own.

My recommendations on your two questions, unchanged from my last message:

1. **`new --publish`: don't run the full `publish` checks.** Those checks protect code you wrote, and a brand-new project only has AIKit's starter files and the LICENSE; the secret scan already runs. The full checks would also refuse every new project, because the starter README keeps a fill-in marker for prerequisites, so the flag would never work. Instead:
   - require `--description` with `--publish`, so a repository is never created without one;
   - state in the help and README that it uploads only the starter files, and that later uploads go through `publish` with its full checks.

2. **OpenCode explorer and architect: yes, remove their shell access.** Their role texts promise read-only, their Claude Code versions already have no shell, and the free models they run on follow "don't write" instructions less reliably. OpenCode's own grep, glob and read tools cover searching; the only loss is `git log`/`git blame`, which the lead agent can supply. I'd avoid allowing just a few safe-looking commands: I couldn't confirm OpenCode checks each part of a chained command, so `git log; python -c …` might slip through.

Say "do both" and I'll implement and test them.
